lessons.title: How 2008 Hit India: Sensex, FIIs, and the IPO Bust

body.text: India was not at the centre of the 2008 crisis, but it was fully connected to it. When global investors desperately needed cash, they sold what they could sell quickly, and Indian shares were easy to sell.

children.text: The previous two lessons followed the crisis from American home loans to the collapse of Lehman Brothers. This lesson follows the shockwave to India. You will see the channels through which a US mortgage problem knocked more than half off the Sensex, weakened the rupee, shut down the IPO market and slowed the economy, how RBI and the government responded, and how the market staged a recovery that almost nobody believed in while it was happening.

markDefs.definition: The belief that an economy, such as India's, could keep growing strongly even as major economies like the US slowed sharply, because its growth was driven mainly by domestic demand.

children.text: In early 2008, a popular view held that India would be largely unaffected by a US slowdown. The economy had grown above 9% a year, domestic consumption was strong, and exports were a smaller share of GDP than in many Asian economies. This idea was called
. It turned out to be half right. India's economy kept growing, but its financial markets were tightly linked to the rest of the world, and the shock arrived through several channels at once.

cells: FIIs sold about ₹52,987 crore of Indian equities in calendar 2008 to raise cash at home
Heavy, persistent selling pressure on the Sensex and Nifty
FII outflows increased demand for dollars
The rupee lost 21.2% against the dollar in 2008-09, from about ₹40.36 to ₹51.23
Overseas borrowing dried up, so Indian companies turned to Indian banks at once
Short-term interest rates spiked and liquidity tightened sharply in October 2008
Export growth fell from about 29% in 2007-08 to about 14% in 2008-09, and turned negative in 2009-10
Falling share prices and global panic hit sentiment
The IPO market shut down, and real estate and capital goods stocks were crushed

body.title: Which Channel Hit First?
body.question: Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September 2008. Which of these channels would have hit Indian markets fastest?
options: Lower exports, as US consumers bought fewer Indian goods
FII selling of Indian shares and the resulting pressure on the rupee
body.explanation: Financial channels move in minutes. FIIs could sell Indian shares and convert rupees into dollars the same day, and the Sensex fell 3.35% on 15 September itself. Trade, GDP and employment effects take months to show up in data. In a global crisis, markets are hit first and the real economy follows.

body.text: FIIs were not selling because they had suddenly lost faith in Indian companies. Many were selling because they faced losses, redemptions and margin calls at home and needed cash. India's large, liquid stocks were among the easiest assets in the world to sell quickly. This is the selling spiral from Lesson 1.3, operating across borders.

children.text: The Rupee: Why ₹40 to ₹51 Is a 21% Fall, Not 27%

Currency moves confuse many investors, so it is worth getting the maths right. The number of rupees needed to buy one dollar rose from about ₹40.36 in March 2008 to ₹51.23 in March 2009. A dollar became about 27% more expensive in rupees. But the rupee's own value fell by a smaller percentage, because we are measuring the fall of the rupee, not the rise of the dollar.

body.latex: \text{Rupee Depreciation (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Old INR per USD}}{\text{New INR per USD}} - 1\right) \times 100
body.caption: Measures how much less one rupee is worth in dollars. A negative result is a depreciation.

body.title: Your Turn: Measure the Rupee's Fall
body.prompt: Using the formula above, calculate the rupee's depreciation against the dollar when it moved from ₹40.36 per dollar to ₹51.23 per dollar. Enter the size of the fall as a positive number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (40.36 ÷ 51.23) minus 1 = about -21.2%, so the rupee lost about 21.2% of its value. That matches the 21.2% depreciation reported in the Economic Survey for 2008-09. Viewed the other way, a dollar became about 26.9% more expensive in rupees. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

children.text: For a foreign investor, the two falls compounded. Take an FII whose Indian shares fell 52% while the rupee lost 21.2%. Measured in dollars, the loss was not 52% but about 62%, because the rupees left over were also worth fewer dollars. That double hit is one reason foreign investors rushed to exit.

The 2007 bull market brought a flood of IPOs, many from real estate, power and infrastructure companies at rich valuations. In Lesson 1.2 you saw Reliance Power's listing day fall in February 2008. That was only the start. The same month, Emaar MGF, a real estate developer, withdrew its IPO of about ₹5,436 crore after lowering its price band twice and extending the bidding period. Wockhardt Hospitals abandoned its IPO after receiving only about 20% subscription.

body.label: The Real Estate Wipeout
body.context: Unitech, then India's second largest property developer, fell about 94% from its level on 10 January 2008, the day the Sensex peaked, to its low in the crisis. DLF fell about 79%. Real estate had been the favourite theme of the 2007 euphoria.

children.text: The financial shock spread into the economy through the second half of 2008. Companies that had borrowed abroad struggled to refinance. Banks, facing a sudden liquidity squeeze in October 2008, became cautious about lending. Mutual funds faced heavy redemptions, especially from corporate investors in liquid and fixed maturity plans, and struggled to sell the short-term paper they held. Exporters in textiles, gems and jewellery, and engineering goods saw orders cancelled. India's GDP growth fell from above 9% in 2007-08 to 6.7% in 2008-09, still strong by global standards in a year when many advanced economies shrank, but a sharp slowdown for India.
How RBI and the Government Responded

Unlike the US, India did not need to rescue failing banks. Its problem was a sudden shortage of liquidity and confidence. RBI and the government responded quickly with a mix of monetary easing, liquidity support and fiscal stimulus.

body.caption: India's Crisis Response, October 2008 to April 2009

cells: Released cash banks had to park with RBI, so they could lend it
Cut the rate at which banks borrow from RBI, lowering borrowing costs
Made parking money with RBI less attractive, pushing banks to lend
Let banks borrow to meet the liquidity needs of mutual funds facing redemptions
Packages on 7 December 2008, 2 January 2009 and February 2009
Included an across-the-board cut of 4 percentage points in central excise duty

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: RBI cut the ___ from 9% to 5%, releasing money that banks were required to keep with the central bank so that they could lend it instead.
body.explanation: The Cash Reserve Ratio is the share of deposits that banks must hold as cash balances with RBI. Cutting it is one of the fastest ways to inject liquidity into the banking system, which is exactly what India needed in late 2008.

columns.label: United States
points: Core problem: insolvent or near insolvent banks and financial firms
Rescued AIG, Bear Stearns and others, and let Lehman fail
$700 billion TARP to inject capital into banks
Policy rate cut to 0% to 0.25% by December 2008

columns.label: India
points: Core problem: a sudden shortage of liquidity and confidence
No major bank failures or bank bailouts needed
Liquidity released through CRR cuts and special repo windows
Repo rate cut from 9% to 4.75% by April 2009
Growth slowed to 6.7% in 2008-09, but no recession

children.text: As global markets bottomed in March 2009 and FIIs began returning, Indian shares rose steadily. Then, on 18 May 2009, the general election result delivered a clear mandate for the incumbent UPA government. The Sensex hit its upper circuit twice within seconds of opening, the first time the index had ever hit an upper circuit, and trading was halted for most of the day. It closed up 2,110.79 points, or about 17.34%, at 14,284.21. By the end of 2009 the Sensex had risen about 81% for the year, and on 5 November 2010, during the Diwali Muhurat trading session, it closed above 21,000 for the first time.

body.label: From the October 2008 Low to November 2010
body.context: The Sensex rose from 8,509.56 to 21,004.96 in just over two years. Investors who sold in panic near the bottom, and waited for "clarity" before buying back, missed much of it.

body.title: October 2008: Sell, Hold or Keep Investing?
body.scenario: It is 27 October 2008. Meera, 34, has ₹8 lakh in equity mutual funds, down about 55% from their value in January. She has a ₹15,000 monthly SIP, a stable job at a pharmaceutical company, and six months of expenses in a fixed deposit. Television anchors are discussing whether India will follow the US into recession. Her brother tells her to stop the SIP, sell everything and move to fixed deposits "until things settle down".
body.prompt: What factors should Meera weigh in deciding what to do? What would have happened to each choice, based on how the market actually behaved afterwards?
body.modelAnswer: Meera's decision should rest on her own situation, not on the headlines. Several factors are in her favour: a stable job in a defensive sector, an emergency fund of six months, no mention of borrowed money, and a long investment horizon at 34. Nothing forces her to sell, so she is not a forced seller in the sense of Lesson 1.3. The key risks to weigh are whether she would need this money in the next few years, and whether she could emotionally tolerate further falls, since no one knew on 27 October that the market had hit its lowest close of the crisis. Looking at what actually followed: selling everything would have locked in a loss of about 55% and, unless she bought back early, missed a rise of over 100% by the end of 2009. Waiting "until things settle down" typically means re-entering after prices have already recovered, since the Sensex jumped about 17% in a single day in May 2009 before most people felt comfortable. Continuing the SIP would have bought units at some of the lowest prices of the decade. Hindsight makes this look easy, and it was not. But the lesson for any future crash is to decide in advance, when calm, what you will do if markets fall 50%, so that the decision is not made by fear on the worst day.

body.title: Build Your Own Crisis Dashboard
steps: Bookmark the NSE page that publishes daily FII and DII buying and selling data, and check it for the last month
Note today's rupee to dollar rate from RBI's reference rate, and compare it with the rate a year ago
Find RBI's current repo rate and CRR, and the date of the next monetary policy meeting
Check the current India VIX, NSE's volatility index, which rises when investors expect bigger swings
Look up the current Nifty 50 PE ratio on the Nifty Indices website, and compare it with its levels in January 2008 and March 2009
Write down, in one paragraph, what you would do with your SIPs and holdings if the Nifty fell 40% from today

cards.definition: The belief that India's growth could stay strong even as the US and Europe slowed sharply. Its financial markets proved tightly coupled in 2008.
Foreign Institutional Investor. FIIs sold about ₹52,987 crore of Indian equities in 2008.

Cash Reserve Ratio: the share of deposits banks must keep with RBI. Cut from 9% to 5% in the crisis.
The rate at which RBI lends to banks. Cut from 9% to 4.75% between October 2008 and April 2009.
The rate RBI paid banks for parking funds with it. Cut from 6% to 3.25% by April 2009.
A trading halt triggered by a sharp rise. The Sensex hit its first ever upper circuit on 18 May 2009.

points: India's economy was not at the centre of the crisis, but its markets were tightly connected to the world, so decoupling proved a myth for investors
The shock reached India through FII selling of about ₹52,987 crore, a 21.2% fall in the rupee, frozen credit, weaker exports and collapsing confidence
The Sensex fell about 60% from its January 2008 peak to its October 2008 low, and about 52% over calendar 2008
The IPO market collapsed: over 90% of 2008 listings traded below issue price, and 2007 and 2008 IPO investors lost about 47% of their money by October 2008
RBI cut CRR from 9% to 5% and the repo rate from 9% to 4.75%, opened special liquidity windows, and the government cut excise duty by 4 percentage points
The recovery was fast and widely doubted: the Sensex rose about 81% in 2009, hit its first ever upper circuit on 18 May 2009, and closed above 21,000 on 5 November 2010
